items.stem: Coolidge's claim that taxation can 'destroy' property rights assumes which view of government revenue?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. Taxation is legitimate only for 'urgent necessity'
B. All taxation is theft
C. Taxes should fund a welfare state
D. Only tariff revenue is constitutional
items.explanation: Coolidge concedes taxation for 'urgent necessity' but treats anything beyond that as destroying the citizen's right to his own industry — the passage's own limiting principle. The other options go further than, or against, his text.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Coolidge concedes taxation for 'urgent necessity' but treats anything beyond that as destroying the citizen's right to enjoy the rewards of his own industry — the passage's own limiting principle.
option_explanations.B: Coolidge did not say all taxation is theft — he allowed taxation for 'urgent necessity.' 'Theft' goes further than his text.
option_explanations.C: Coolidge did not say taxes should fund a welfare state — his whole argument limits taxation to urgent necessity, the opposite of a welfare state.
option_explanations.D: Coolidge did not argue only tariff revenue is constitutional — his address was about taxation in general, not about restricting revenue to tariffs.

items.stem: Coolidge's warning against heavy taxation most directly continued the tradition of
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. Hamiltonian support for a national bank
B. Jeffersonian opposition to energetic federal government
C. Jacksonian enthusiasm for internal improvements
D. Whig support for the American System
items.explanation: Coolidge's small-government creed descends from Jeffersonian strict construction — the founding-era suspicion of energetic federal power. Hamilton, the Whigs, and Jackson (on internal improvements) all favored a more active federal role.

option_explanations.A: Hamilton supported a national bank and energetic federal power — the opposite tradition from Coolidge's small-government creed.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Coolidge's small-government creed descends from Jeffersonian strict construction — the founding-era suspicion of energetic federal power.
option_explanations.C: Jackson's enthusiasm for internal improvements (in his early career) favored federal action — not the tradition Coolidge's warning continues.
option_explanations.D: Whig support for the American System meant an active federal role in banking, tariffs, and improvements — the opposite of Coolidge's creed.

items.stem: Coolidge's confidence that low taxes and limited government produce prosperity was shaken most directly by
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. World War II
B. The Cold War
C. The Great Depression
D. The civil rights movement
items.explanation: The Great Depression shattered Coolidge's formula — prosperity did not return when government stayed out, and voters demanded the activist state he had warned against. World War II, the Cold War, and civil rights came later or addressed different questions.

option_explanations.A: World War II did not shake Coolidge's formula — it ended the Depression through massive government spending, but the Depression itself was what discredited his creed.
option_explanations.B: The Cold War came later and addressed foreign policy, not the question of whether limited government produces prosperity.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Great Depression shattered Coolidge's formula — prosperity did not return when government stayed out, and voters demanded the activist state he had warned against.
option_explanations.D: The civil rights movement addressed racial justice, not the economic question of whether low taxes and limited government produce prosperity.

items.stem: Coolidge's argument would be weakest against which criticism?
items.stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

In a 1924 address, President Calvin Coolidge argued that people have a right to enjoy the rewards of their own industry, warning that heavy taxation on property or income amounts to destroying that right. —Paraphrase of Calvin Coolidge, "Economy in the Interest of All," June 30, 1924 (abridged)
options: A. That the income tax is unconstitutional
B. That Britain levied higher taxes
C. That farmers opposed protective tariffs
D. That an industrial nation needs public goods only government can provide
items.explanation: The hard question for Coolidge's creed is the public-goods problem: industrial America needed roads, regulation, and services that only government could provide at scale. The other options are false or irrelevant to his argument.

option_explanations.A: That the income tax is unconstitutional is false — the Sixteenth Amendment (1913) authorized it. A false claim is not the strongest criticism.
option_explanations.B: That Britain levied higher taxes is irrelevant — what other countries did does not answer Coolidge's argument about American property rights.
option_explanations.C: That farmers opposed protective tariffs is beside the point — Coolidge's argument is about taxation and property rights generally, not about farm views on tariffs.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the criticism Coolidge's argument is weakest against. The public-goods problem is real: an industrial nation needs roads, regulation, and services that only government can provide at scale, and Coolidge's creed offers no answer for them.

items.stem: Which of the following most directly reflects de Bry's perspective in the image?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]

options.text: The natives of Florida are primitive and superstitious.
The natives of Florida are deeply Christian.
Europeans are unjustly exploiting the natives.
Conflict between natives and Europeans is inevitable.

items.explanation: De Bry shows the Timucua worshipping a French monument, framing them as simple people awed by European symbols. The image flatters European power rather than criticizing it or predicting war.

option_explanations.A: Correct. De Bry shows the Timucua kneeling in worship before a French monument, framing them as simple people awed by European symbols — the image presents them as primitive and superstitious.
option_explanations.B: The image does not show the Timucua as Christian — they are shown worshipping a French column, not practicing Christianity.
option_explanations.C: The image does not criticize European exploitation — it flatters European power, showing natives awed by French symbols. Critique is the opposite of its perspective.
option_explanations.D: The image does not predict inevitable conflict — it shows peaceful awe and submission, not clashing armies.

items.stem: De Bry's engraving is best understood as an expression of which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]

options.text: European doubts about the value of exploration
European curiosity about the wider world

items.explanation: De Bry produced dozens of engravings of New World peoples for a European audience hungry for news of the Americas. The image feeds curiosity about distant lands and peoples, not fear of them or doubt about exploration.

option_explanations.A: The image does not express fear of native peoples — the Timucua are shown kneeling in worship, not as a threat. Fear is absent from the scene.
option_explanations.B: The image does not express religious fervor — it is about European curiosity and display, not about religious devotion.
option_explanations.C: The image does not express doubt about exploration — de Bry's whole Grand Voyages enterprise celebrated New World discovery. Doubt is the opposite of its purpose.
option_explanations.D: Correct. De Bry produced dozens of engravings of New World peoples for a European audience hungry for news of the Americas — the image feeds curiosity about distant lands and peoples.

option_explanations.B: The column was not about trade hopes — Ribault's column announced French sovereignty, not commercial plans.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Ribault's column was a marker of possession: a public claim that France owned the land — the legal basis European powers used to announce sovereignty over new territory.

items.stem: Rivalries among European powers soon led the French settlement in Florida to be destroyed by which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 5–8 refer to the following image.

[An engraving by Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591: a stone column stands on a Florida shore while a crowd of Timucua Native Americans kneel before it in worship, as French soldiers and officers look on.]
items.explanation: Spain, which claimed Florida, attacked the French Huguenot colony at Fort Caroline in 1565 and massacred its inhabitants. Neither the English nor the Dutch operated in Florida at that time.

option_explanations.A: The Timucua did not destroy the French settlement — the attackers were the Spanish, who claimed Florida and massacred the French Huguenots at Fort Caroline in 1565.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Spain, which claimed Florida, attacked the French Huguenot colony at Fort Caroline in 1565 and massacred its inhabitants.
option_explanations.C: The English did not destroy the French Florida settlement — England had no presence in Florida in 1565.
option_explanations.D: The Dutch did not destroy the French Florida settlement — the Netherlands had no presence in Florida at that time.

items.stem: Riis's purpose in detailing the woman's wages and meals was to
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
options: A. Praise the woman's thrift and industry
B. Shock comfortable readers into demanding reform
C. Recruit workers for the factory
D. Defend tenement landlords
items.explanation: Riis itemizes her wages, rent, and single daily meal to horrify comfortable readers into demanding reform — the muckraker's method. He neither praises her thrift nor defends her landlords.

option_explanations.A: Riis did not praise the woman's thrift — he detailed her $3-a-week wages and single daily meal to horrify readers, not to celebrate her industry.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Riis itemizes her wages, rent, and single daily meal to shock comfortable readers into demanding reform — the muckraker's method.
option_explanations.C: Riis did not recruit workers for the factory — his exposé attacked factory conditions, the opposite of recruiting for them.
option_explanations.D: Riis did not defend tenement landlords — his whole project indicted the conditions landlords profited from.

items.stem: Riis's 'slavery' metaphor for the woman's working conditions most directly recalled the rhetoric of
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
options: A. Antebellum labor activists who denounced 'wage slavery'
B. Southern planters defending slavery
C. Confederate generals
D. Abolitionists defending the Fugitive Slave Act
items.explanation: Antebellum labor activists — including the Lowell mill women — called industrial exploitation 'wage slavery,' the exact metaphor Riis reaches for. Planters and Confederates defended slavery; abolitionists never defended the Fugitive Slave Act.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Antebellum labor activists — including the Lowell mill women — called industrial exploitation 'wage slavery,' the exact metaphor Riis reaches for.
option_explanations.B: Southern planters defended slavery — they would never call factory labor 'slavery' as a criticism. Planters used the comparison to claim their slaves were better off.
option_explanations.C: Confederate generals fought for slavery — they did not denounce wage slavery. The metaphor belongs to labor activists, not Confederates.
option_explanations.D: Abolitionists never defended the Fugitive Slave Act — they attacked it. And Riis's metaphor comes from labor rhetoric, not abolitionism.

items.stem: Riis's exposé relied on which new technology to make its case?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
options: A. The telegraph
B. Radio broadcasts
C. Motion pictures with sound
D. Flash photography documenting tenement interiors
items.explanation: Riis pioneered flash photography to document dark tenement interiors — the visual evidence that made How the Other Half Lives undeniable. The telegraph, radio, and sound film played no role in his 1890 exposé.

option_explanations.A: The telegraph played no role in Riis's exposé — his breakthrough was visual, not in long-distance communication.
option_explanations.B: Radio broadcasts did not exist in 1890 — Riis's book predates radio by decades.
option_explanations.C: Motion pictures with sound did not exist in 1890 — Riis's medium was photography, not film.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Riis pioneered flash photography to document dark tenement interiors — the visual evidence that made How the Other Half Lives undeniable.

items.stem: The passage's detailed account of one woman's budget exemplifies which journalistic technique?
items.stimulus:
Questions 9–12 refer to the following quotation.

"Here is the case of a woman employed in the manufacturing department of a Broadway house. … She averages three dollars a week. … lunch she cannot afford. One meal a day is her allowance. … Almost any door might seem to offer a welcome escape from such slavery as this." —Jacob Riis, How the Other Half Lives, 1890 (abridged)
options: A. Publishing government statistics
B. Endorsing political candidates
C. Using one person's story to illustrate a widespread problem
D. Writing fictional short stories
items.explanation: Riis builds his whole case from one woman's budget — the representative-case technique of making a systemic problem visible through a single life. He publishes no statistics, endorses no candidates, and writes nonfiction.

option_explanations.A: Riis did not publish government statistics — his technique was the representative individual case, not data tables.
option_explanations.B: Riis did not endorse political candidates — he was a journalist and reformer, not a campaigner.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Riis builds his whole case from one woman's budget — using one person's story to illustrate a widespread problem, the representative-case technique.
option_explanations.D: Riis did not write fiction — How the Other Half Lives was documentary nonfiction, built from real cases and photographs.

items.stem: The Zenger trial arose most directly from
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. Printed criticism of New York's royal governor
B. A dispute over British taxation
C. An attack on the institution of slavery
D. A religious controversy
items.explanation: Zenger's Weekly Journal printed attacks on New York's royal governor Cosby, who had him prosecuted for seditious libel. Taxation, slavery, and religion were not at issue in the 1735 trial.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Zenger's Weekly Journal printed attacks on New York's royal governor Cosby, who had him prosecuted for seditious libel. Taxation, slavery, and religion were not at issue in the 1735 trial.
option_explanations.B: The trial was not about British taxation — Zenger was prosecuted for criticizing Governor Cosby, not for a tax dispute.
option_explanations.C: The trial was not about slavery — the issue was criticism of the royal governor, not the institution of slavery.
option_explanations.D: The trial was not about religion — no religious controversy was involved. The charge was seditious libel against the governor.

items.stem: Hamilton's claim that complaining when hurt is 'a right which all free men claim' draws most directly on
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. French absolutist theory
B. The traditional liberties of English subjects
C. Spanish colonial law
D. Native American diplomacy
items.explanation: Hamilton appeals to the inherited liberties of English subjects — the common-law tradition that free men may complain of abuses. He invokes no French, Spanish, or Native legal tradition.

option_explanations.A: French absolutist theory supported unlimited royal power — the opposite of Hamilton's claim that free men may complain when hurt.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Hamilton appeals to the inherited liberties of English subjects — the common-law tradition that free men may complain of abuses.
option_explanations.C: Hamilton invoked no Spanish colonial law — his appeal was to English liberties, not Spanish legal tradition.
option_explanations.D: Hamilton invoked no Native American diplomacy — his framework was English common law, not Indigenous tradition.

items.stem: Unlike the Pentagon Papers case, the Zenger trial is most notable for establishing its principle through
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. An act of Parliament
B. A presidential pardon
C. A jury's verdict rather than an appellate ruling
D. A constitutional amendment
items.explanation: Zenger won his freedom from a colonial jury that refused to convict — jury nullification established the principle. The Pentagon Papers principle came from the Supreme Court in New York Times v. United States (1971), not from a jury.

option_explanations.A: No act of Parliament established the Zenger principle — the acquittal came from a colonial jury, not from legislation.
option_explanations.B: No presidential pardon was involved — Zenger was acquitted by a jury in 1735, a century before the presidency's pardon power could apply.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Zenger won his freedom from a colonial jury that refused to convict — jury nullification established the principle. The Pentagon Papers principle, by contrast, came from the Supreme Court in New York Times v. United States (1971), not from a jury.
option_explanations.D: No constitutional amendment established the principle — the acquittal was a jury verdict in 1735, decades before the Constitution existed.

items.stem: The jury's acquittal of Zenger demonstrated that colonial juries could
items.stimulus:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following quotation.

"It is … a right, which all free men claim, that they are entitled to complain when they are hurt. … It is not the cause of one poor printer, nor of New York alone … It is the cause of liberty." —Andrew Hamilton, defense of printer John Peter Zenger, August 4, 1735 (abridged)
options: A. Levy taxes on the colonists
B. Declare independence from Britain
C. Enforce the Navigation Acts
D. Serve as a check on royal authority
items.explanation: The acquittal showed a colonial jury defying the royal governor's handpicked judges — the jury as a popular check on imperial authority. Juries levied no taxes, declared no independence, and enforced no trade acts.

option_explanations.A: Colonial juries did not levy taxes — taxation was the assembly's and Parliament's business, not the jury's.
option_explanations.B: The jury did not declare independence — that came forty years later. The acquittal was a check on the governor, not a revolution.
option_explanations.C: The jury did not enforce the Navigation Acts — those were enforced by vice-admiralty courts, often against colonial wishes.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The acquittal showed a colonial jury defying the royal governor's handpicked judges — the jury serving as a popular check on imperial authority.

items.stem: Which of the following best expresses Thomas Nast's perspective in the cartoon?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The Reconstruction of the South is succeeding.
The government is failing to protect freed Black people.
Reconstructing Southern society was a mistake.

items.explanation: Nast shows armed white-supremacist groups terrorizing a Black family, warning that freedpeople are being returned to something 'worse than slavery.' He is demanding stronger federal protection, not celebrating Reconstruction.

option_explanations.A: Nast's cartoon does not show Reconstruction succeeding — it shows white-supremacist terror, a warning that freedpeople face something 'worse than slavery.'
option_explanations.B: Correct. Nast shows armed White League and Klan members terrorizing a Black family — his perspective is that the government is failing to protect freed Black people, and he demands stronger federal action.
option_explanations.C: Nast does not argue white Southerners must stand together — the handshake across a skull is his condemnation of white-supremacist unity, not an endorsement.
option_explanations.D: Nast does not argue Reconstruction was a mistake — he argues it is being betrayed. His demand is for more federal protection, not abandonment.

items.stem: The conditions Nast depicts contributed most directly to which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The Homestead Act offering settlers free land
The Supreme Court's Plessy v. Ferguson decision

items.explanation: The failure to stop white-supremacist violence left segregation to harden into law, culminating in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which upheld 'separate but equal.' The Fifteenth Amendment predates the cartoon; the Homestead Act is unrelated.

option_explanations.A: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) predates the 1874 cartoon — the violence Nast depicts came after it. The amendment could not be its product.
option_explanations.B: The Homestead Act was about western settlement — unrelated to the white-supremacist violence Nast depicts in the South.
option_explanations.C: The New South industrialization movement was an economic program, not the product of the terror Nast depicts.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The failure to stop white-supremacist violence left segregation to harden into law, culminating in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), which upheld 'separate but equal.'

items.stem: The Southerners in the cartoon wanted a 'Union' in which sovereignty rested with which of the following?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: The anti-nullification nationalism of Andrew Jackson.

items.explanation: Nast's 'Union as it was' is the states'-rights Union of the Lost Cause: each state supreme within its borders, free to subordinate Black citizens. That doctrine had justified slavery before the war and segregation after it.

option_explanations.A: The federal government was what the Southerners wanted to resist, not what they wanted sovereignty to rest with — their 'Union as it was' limited federal power.
option_explanations.B: The American System of internal improvements was Clay's nationalist program, not the Southern states'-rights doctrine. Nast's 'Union as it was' is the opposite tradition.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Nast's 'Union as it was' is the states'-rights Union of the Lost Cause: each state supreme within its borders, free to subordinate Black citizens — the doctrine that had justified slavery before the war and segregation after it.
option_explanations.D: Andrew Jackson's anti-nullification nationalism asserted federal supremacy — the opposite of what the cartoon's Southerners wanted. Their 'Union as it was' rejected Jackson's nationalism.

items.stem: Nast's cartoon most directly reflects the continuity of which of the following debates in U.S. history?
items.stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A political cartoon by Thomas Nast, 'The Union as It Was / The Lost Cause, Worse Than Slavery,' Harper's Weekly, October 24, 1874: members of the White League and the Ku Klux Klan shake hands across a skull, while a Black family cowes in terror beneath them.]

options.text: Debates over the use of military power
Debates over the role of political parties

items.explanation: Nast was intervening in the struggle over Black Americans' rights, a debate running from slavery through Reconstruction to the modern civil rights era. The cartoon says nothing about the military, guns, or parties as institutions.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Nast was intervening in the struggle over Black Americans' rights — a debate running from slavery through Reconstruction to the modern civil rights era. The cartoon says nothing about the military, guns, or parties as institutions.
option_explanations.B: The cartoon does not debate military power — its subject is white-supremacist terror and federal failure to protect freedpeople, not the armed forces.
option_explanations.C: The cartoon does not debate gun control — the weapons are symbols of terror, not the subject of a policy debate.
option_explanations.D: The cartoon does not debate the role of political parties — its subject is the civil-rights struggle, not party institutions.

items.stem: The 1984 Democratic ticket's selection of a woman for vice president most directly responded to
items.stimulus:

options.text: A charter colony, in which the king granted a charter to colonists
A proprietary colony governed by a proprietor
A royal colony, in which the king appointed the governor
An independent colony operating outside the king's authority

items.explanation: Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William Penn personally, making it a proprietary colony: Penn and his heirs owned and governed it. It was neither a corporate charter colony, a royal colony, nor independent of the crown.

option_explanations.A: Pennsylvania was not a charter colony — Charles II granted it to William Penn personally as a proprietorship, not to a corporate body of colonists.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Charles II granted Pennsylvania to William Penn personally, making it a proprietary colony: Penn and his heirs owned and governed it.
option_explanations.C: Pennsylvania was not a royal colony in this period — the king did not appoint its governor. It was proprietary, not royal.
option_explanations.D: Pennsylvania was not independent of the crown — Penn held his grant from Charles II. Independence was never its status.

option_explanations.D: Pennsylvania was not hostile to religious practice — the Charter welcomed faith. Hostility to religion was the opposite of its reputation.

items.stem: Penn's Charter of Privileges is best seen as a forerunner of which of the following?

options.text: The First Amendment to the Constitution

items.explanation: By barring an established church and protecting conscience, the Charter anticipated the First Amendment's religion clauses. The Declaration announced independence; the Fourteen Points and Gettysburg Address address different subjects.

option_explanations.A: The Declaration of Independence announced independence in 1776 — the Charter of Privileges was about religious toleration and representative government, not independence.

option_explanations.C: The Gettysburg Address was about the Civil War and equality — not about religious toleration. Different subject, different century.
option_explanations.D: Correct. By barring an established church and protecting conscience, the Charter anticipated the First Amendment's religion clauses.

items.stem: Henry Adams's portrait of the awkward, shy Jefferson serves his larger point that

options: A. Jefferson was unfit for office

option_explanations.B: Correct. Adams's irony is the point: this awkward, shy man was among 'the controlling influences of American history' — proof that vast historical forces work through unlikely individuals.
option_explanations.C: Adams did not admire Jefferson without reservation — his portrait is ironical, noting Jefferson's limitations even while acknowledging his historical weight.
option_explanations.D: Adams does not argue appearance determines destiny — his point is the opposite: an unimpressive-looking man channeled great historical forces.

items.stem: Jefferson's 'Revolution of 1800' reversed Federalist policies by

items.explanation: The 'Revolution of 1800' was a policy revolution: Jefferson shrank the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, and attacked the national debt. He built no new bank, raised no tariffs, and made no war on France.

option_explanations.A: Jefferson did not expand the navy or raise tariffs — he shrank the military and repealed internal taxes. Expansion was the opposite of his program.
option_explanations.B: Jefferson did not create a new national bank — he opposed the Bank of the United States and let its influence wane. A new bank was never his policy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The 'Revolution of 1800' was a policy revolution: Jefferson shrank the army and navy, repealed internal taxes, and attacked the national debt.
option_explanations.D: Jefferson did not declare war on France — he pursued peace and bought Louisiana from Napoleon. War with France was never his policy.

items.stem: Jefferson's Louisiana Purchase contradicted his strict constructionism because
items.stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"The man who mounted the steps of the Capitol, March 4, 1801 … Jefferson was very tall, six feet two-and-a-half inches in height; sandy-complexioned; shy in manner, seeming cold; awkward in attitude … this loose, shackling person … belonged to the controlling influences of American history." —Henry Adams, History of the United States During the Administration of Thomas Jefferson, 1889 (abridged)
options: A. France refused to sell Louisiana
B. Congress unanimously opposed the purchase
C. It expanded slavery into New England
D. The Constitution nowhere authorized purchasing foreign territory
items.explanation: Strict construction gave Jefferson no clear authority to buy foreign territory — he admitted the Constitution 'has made no provision for our holding foreign territory,' yet bought Louisiana anyway. France was eager to sell, and Congress approved.

option_explanations.A: France did not refuse to sell Louisiana — Napoleon was eager to sell. The contradiction is constitutional, not diplomatic.
option_explanations.B: Congress did not unanimously oppose the purchase — it approved it. The contradiction is with Jefferson's own strict constructionism, not with Congress.
option_explanations.C: The purchase did not expand slavery into New England — Louisiana was in the South and West. The constitutional issue was the lack of authority to buy foreign territory.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Strict construction gave Jefferson no clear authority to buy foreign territory — he admitted the Constitution 'has made no provision for our holding foreign territory,' yet bought Louisiana anyway.

items.stem: Adams's depiction of Washington as a cultural backwater illustrates

"The man who mounted the steps of the Capitol, March 4, 1801 … Jefferson was very tall, six feet two-and-a-half inches in height; sandy-complexioned; shy in manner, seeming cold; awkward in attitude … this loose, shackling person … belonged to the controlling influences of American history." —Henry Adams, History of the United States During the Administration of Thomas Jefferson, 1889 (abridged)
options: A. How new and unformed the national government still was
B. British cultural superiority over America

items.explanation: Adams's village-capital — politicians 'living like bears' without court or commerce — shows a national government still inventing itself from nothing. It illustrates newness, not British superiority, industry, or Southern dominance.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Adams's village-capital — politicians 'living like bears' without court or commerce — shows a national government still inventing itself from nothing, new and unformed.
option_explanations.B: Adams does not argue British cultural superiority — his point is about the newness of the American government, not about Britain's advantages.
option_explanations.C: Washington was not industrializing — Adams depicts a muddy village, not factories. Industrialization is the opposite of his image.
option_explanations.D: Adams does not depict Southern economic dominance — his subject is the unformed national capital, not sectional economics.

items.stem: Roosevelt addressed the ACLU in March 1940 because

options: A. She supported the internment of Japanese Americans
B. She feared war would again erode civil liberties as in World War I
C. The ACLU had opposed the New Deal
D. The Cold War had already begun
items.explanation: Roosevelt spoke to the ACLU as Europe went to war because she feared a repeat of 1917–18, when dissent was criminalized — the motive for her warning. She never supported internment, the ACLU backed civil liberties, and the Cold War had not begun.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt never supported the internment of Japanese Americans — she was one of the administration's internal critics of it. Support was the opposite of her position.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Roosevelt spoke to the ACLU as Europe went to war because she feared a repeat of 1917–18, when dissent was criminalized — the motive for her warning that Americans must guard civil liberties.
option_explanations.C: The ACLU did not oppose the New Deal — it was a civil-liberties organization, and Roosevelt addressed it on liberties, not on New Deal politics.
option_explanations.D: The Cold War had not begun in March 1940 — it started after World War II. Roosevelt's concern was a repeat of World War I's repression.

option_explanations.B: The Whiskey Ring was an 1870s tax-fraud scandal — it involved no civil-liberties crisis.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Second Red Scare's loyalty-security programs — blacklists, loyalty oaths, HUAC hearings — vindicated Roosevelt's warning that crises endanger liberty.
option_explanations.D: The Freedmen's Bureau was a Reconstruction aid agency — it involved no civil-liberties crisis of the kind Roosevelt warned about.

items.stem: Like Roosevelt in 1940, critics of the Patriot Act argued that

In a March 14, 1940 address to the American Civil Liberties Union, Eleanor Roosevelt said that traveling the country had made her conscious of the importance of civil liberties, warned that democracy is endangered whenever the light of liberty grows dim, and argued that while wartime nations lose freedoms of press, speech, and assembly, Americans at peace had a grave responsibility to guard them. —Paraphrase of Eleanor Roosevelt, address to the ACLU, Chicago, March 14, 1940 (abridged)
options: A. Civil liberties are unimportant in wartime

items.explanation: Both Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics make the same argument: fear and crisis tempt even free governments to trade liberty for security. Neither side claims liberties are unimportant or that the ACLU should vanish.

option_explanations.A: Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics never claimed civil liberties are unimportant in wartime — they claimed the opposite: liberties must be guarded precisely when crisis tempts their surrender.
option_explanations.B: Neither side claimed only wartime justifies free speech — their argument is that liberty must be defended in peacetime too, against the temptations of crisis.
option_explanations.C: Neither side called for abolishing the ACLU — Roosevelt was addressing the ACLU as an ally, and the Patriot Act's critics invoked the same liberties the ACLU defends.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Both Roosevelt and the Patriot Act's critics make the same argument: fear and crisis tempt even free governments to trade liberty for security.
